guides.title: Making Soap: Saponification, Lye Math & Safety
guides.summary: How soap is made from fats and lye, with the chemistry of saponification, exact lye-calculation math using SAP values, and the safety discipline required to handle sodium hydroxide.

sections.heading: What Soap Is and the Saponification Reaction
sections.body:
Soap is the salt of a fatty acid, and everything else about soapmaking follows from that one sentence. Fats and oils are triglycerides: three long fatty-acid chains joined by ester bonds to a single three-carbon glycerol backbone. A strong alkali attacks those ester bonds, splits the chains away from the backbone, and leaves each chain as the salt of its acid. The reaction is called saponification, from the Latin sapo, soap. In words it reads fat or oil plus lye gives soap plus glycerol, and written properly for sodium hydroxide it is one triglyceride plus 3 NaOH giving 3 molecules of R-COONa plus C₃H₅(OH)₃, glycerol. The stoichiometry matters: three moles of alkali per mole of fat, because there are three ester bonds to break. This is the reason lye quantity is calculated rather than estimated. 

The soap molecule R-COONa is what does the cleaning, and its structure explains why. R is a hydrocarbon tail typically 12 to 18 carbons long, non-polar and therefore oil-loving, or hydrophobic. The -COONa carboxylate head is ionic and therefore water-loving, or hydrophilic. A molecule with both ends is called a surfactant, short for surface-active agent. Dropped into water with grease present, these molecules spontaneously arrange into tiny spheres called micelles, tails pointed inward into the oil droplet, ionic heads outward into the water. The grease is now wrapped in a water-compatible shell and rinses away. Soap does not dissolve dirt; it suspends it. 

Two alkalis are used in practice, and they are not interchangeable. Sodium hydroxide, NaOH, also sold as caustic soda, produces a hard bar. Potassium hydroxide, KOH, caustic potash, produces soft, cream, or liquid soap, because the potassium salt of a fatty acid is considerably more soluble than the sodium salt. Substituting one for the other without recalculating guarantees failure: NaOH is 40.0 grams per mole and KOH is 56.1, so a given mass of KOH contains far fewer hydroxide ions than the same mass of NaOH. Roughly 1.40 grams of KOH does the work of 1 gram of NaOH. 

The glycerol produced alongside the soap is not waste. It is a humectant, meaning it draws moisture from the air, and in handmade soap it stays in the bar, which is much of why handmade soap feels less drying than an industrial detergent bar from which the glycerol has been extracted and sold separately. 

The same carboxylate head that makes soap work is also its one real weakness. In hard water, dissolved calcium and magnesium ions displace the sodium and form calcium and magnesium stearate, salts that are essentially insoluble. These precipitate as the grey curd known as soap scum, the ring around a bath and the stiffness in laundered towels, and every molecule tied up that way is a molecule no longer available to lift grease, which is why soap lathers poorly in hard water. Synthetic detergents were developed largely to solve this specific problem, using head groups such as sulphonates whose calcium salts stay dissolved. Historically the alkali came from leaching wood ash, which yields potassium carbonate rather than hydroxide and gives a weaker, less predictable soft soap.

sections.heading: SAP Values and the Core Lye Calculation
sections.body:
Every fat requires a specific quantity of alkali to be fully converted, and that quantity is fixed by chemistry, not by preference. The number that encodes it is the saponification value, universally abbreviated SAP: the milligrams of potassium hydroxide required to saponify one gram of that particular fat. It is expressed for KOH by long-standing analytical convention, which is why most published charts give KOH figures even though most bar soap is made with sodium hydroxide. A high SAP value means the fat is built from short fatty-acid chains, so one gram contains more ester bonds and therefore demands more alkali; a low SAP means long chains and fewer bonds per gram. 

Typical published values, in milligrams of KOH per gram of oil, run approximately as follows: olive oil 190, coconut oil 257, palm oil 199, beef tallow 200, lard 195, and castor oil 180. Coconut oil sits highest on that list precisely because it is dominated by lauric acid at twelve carbons, a short chain, so a gram of it holds substantially more reactive ester groups than a gram of oleic-rich olive oil. Note that all of these are ranges in reality rather than constants; the fatty-acid composition of a natural fat varies with the crop, the animal, the season, and the refining process, so charts differ by a few percent between sources. This variability is one of the reasons a safety margin is built into every recipe rather than working to the exact theoretical figure. 

Converting a KOH SAP value into the sodium hydroxide figure you actually need is a single division by the ratio of the two molar masses, 56.1 divided by 40.0, which equals 1.403. Expressed as a usable factor, the NaOH requirement in grams per gram of oil equals the KOH SAP in milligrams per gram, divided by 1000 to convert milligrams to grams, then divided by 1.403. Olive oil worked through: 190 milligrams per gram becomes 0.190 grams of KOH per gram of oil, and 0.190 divided by 1.403 gives 0.1354 grams of NaOH per gram of oil. 

The final step is simple multiplication. The lye required in grams equals the oil weight in grams multiplied by that NaOH factor. For 500 grams of olive oil, 500 times 0.1354 is 67.7 grams of NaOH, and that figure represents complete saponification with no fat and no alkali left over. In a blend, each oil is calculated separately against its own factor and the results are summed, because the oils do not average; a 70/30 blend needs the 70 percent oil's requirement plus the 30 percent oil's requirement, computed independently and added. Forgetting the 1.403 conversion is the single most common arithmetic error in the craft, and it produces a bar with roughly 40 percent excess alkali, which is caustic enough to injure skin.

sections.heading: Superfat, Lye Concentration & Water
sections.body:
Superfatting, also called a lye discount, means deliberately using slightly less alkali than the stoichiometric calculation demands, so that a small fraction of the oil survives the reaction unsaponified. The reason is asymmetry of risk. Excess free fatty acid in a bar makes it milder and more conditioning, and the worst outcome of overdoing it is a soft bar with a shortened shelf life. Excess free alkali makes a bar that is chemically caustic and will burn skin. Since natural fats vary in composition, published SAP charts disagree slightly, and kitchen scales have real tolerances, a deliberate margin on the safe side absorbs all three error sources at once. Five percent is the near-universal default for a bar soap. Three percent suits a harder, more cleansing recipe; eight to twenty percent suits facial and shaving bars, at the cost of a softer bar that can go rancid sooner. The arithmetic is one multiplication: superfatted lye equals full lye multiplied by one minus the superfat fraction. For the 500-gram olive oil case requiring 67.7 grams at zero superfat, five percent gives 67.7 times 0.95, which is 64.3 grams of NaOH. 

It is worth understanding what superfat does not control. It does not choose which oil is left behind. In cold process the alkali reacts preferentially with whichever fatty acids it encounters fastest, so the surviving fraction is a mixture weighted toward the slower-reacting long-chain acids, not the expensive shea butter you hoped to reserve. Only in hot process, where additives go in after the reaction has essentially finished, can you genuinely choose the superfat oil. 

Water is a solvent, not a reactant. It exists to dissolve the solid alkali into a pourable solution that can emulsify evenly into the oils, and almost all of it eventually evaporates during cure. The modern way to specify it is by lye concentration, meaning the alkali's percentage of the combined lye-plus-water solution by mass. Thirty-three percent is a reliable, forgiving default. The formula is water in grams equals lye in grams divided by 0.33, minus the lye in grams. For 64.3 grams of lye: 64.3 divided by 0.33 gives a total solution of 194.8 grams, so the water is 194.8 minus 64.3, which is 130.5 grams. The older beginner shorthand of water equal to twice the lye by weight is the same thing at 33.3 percent concentration, and here gives 128.6 grams, close enough to be interchangeable. A stronger solution, meaning less water, traces faster, gels more readily, and cures quicker but leaves less working time; a weaker solution does the opposite and risks a soft, slow-setting bar. 

Work exclusively in mass, never in volume. Oils, lye solution, and water all have different densities, and a cup of coconut oil and a cup of olive oil are not the same quantity of reactive material. A digital scale reading to one gram is the minimum, and 0.1 gram resolution is better for batches under a kilogram. Never estimate lye: too much leaves a caustic bar that injures skin, and too much excess fat leaves a soft bar that turns rancid.

sections.heading: Cold-Process Procedure, Step by Step
sections.body:
Cold process is the standard home method, and its name misleads: nothing is chilled, it simply means no external heat drives the reaction, which completes slowly in the mould and over the following weeks. A representative starter batch is 500 grams of oil split 350 olive and 150 coconut, each calculated against its own factor and summed, landing near 71 grams of sodium hydroxide at five percent superfat with roughly 142 grams of distilled water. Re-derive those figures rather than borrowing them; a transcription error in the lye weight is the one mistake with real consequences. 

Preparation comes first because the reactive steps allow no pauses. Wear splash goggles, elbow-length chemical gloves, and long sleeves, and set up where air moves freely: outdoors, an open garage, or a kitchen with the extractor running. Keep vinegar within reach for neutralising alkali spilled on work surfaces, and understand that vinegar is for surfaces, not skin; skin gets flooded with running water instead, because neutralising an alkali on injured tissue releases heat and compounds the burn. 

The alkali always goes into the water, never the reverse. Pouring water onto a mass of solid lye concentrates the heat of dissolution in a thin layer at the surface, which can flash to steam and erupt the whole vessel. Sprinkle the pellets into the water gradually while stirring, and expect the solution to climb to roughly 90 °C within a minute purely from dissolution, releasing a sharp fume for the first thirty seconds or so. Do not lean over it. Set it aside to cool toward 40 °C. 

Meanwhile melt the solid fats just enough to liquefy them, coconut oil melting around 24 °C, then stir in the liquid oils and bring the pot to roughly the same 40 °C. Getting both within five to ten degrees of each other matters: a large difference either shocks the fats into partial solidification, producing lumps that never saponify, or accelerates the reaction into a runaway. 

Pour the lye solution into the oils and blend with a stick blender in short bursts, alternating with hand stirring so the motor does not whip in air. You are looking for trace: the mixture has emulsified into a stable single phase with the consistency of thin pudding, and a drizzle from the blender leaves a visible trail on the surface for a second before sinking. Trace is an emulsion endpoint, not a completion signal; saponification has barely begun. Any fragrance, essential oil at around three percent of the oil weight, or colourant goes in at trace, quickly, because some fragrances accelerate thickening dramatically. 

Pour into a silicone or lined mould, rap it on the bench to release trapped air, and cover with a towel for 24 to 48 hours so the batch retains its own reaction heat. Unmould and cut into bars once firm, then cure on an airy rack for four to six weeks, turning occasionally. Curing is water evaporating and the last of the reaction finishing; the difference between a two-week bar and a six-week bar is genuinely noticeable in hardness, mildness, and how long it lasts.

sections.heading: Testing, Common Mistakes & Troubleshooting
sections.body:
A finished bar should be tested before it touches anyone's skin, because a calculation error is invisible in the mould. Cured handmade soap is mildly alkaline by nature, typically pH 9 to 10, since the salt of a weak acid and a strong base hydrolyses slightly in water; a soap at pH 7 is chemically impossible and any product claiming it is a synthetic detergent, not soap. The value that signals danger is above roughly 11, which indicates free unreacted hydroxide. Wet the bar, press a pH strip against the lather rather than the dry surface, and read it against the chart. 

The traditional check is the zap test: touch the tip of the tongue briefly to a cut face of the bar. Free alkali produces an unmistakable electric tingle, much like touching a nine-volt battery terminal, caused by ion conduction across the tongue. Safe soap tastes soapy and faintly bitter with no tingle at all. It is a genuinely useful test used throughout the craft, but it is a deliberate contact with a possibly caustic surface, so touch briefly, rinse, and use pH strips instead if the batch is under any suspicion at all. 

The recurring mistakes fall into a short list. Using the KOH saponification value directly without dividing by 1.403 produces about 40 percent excess alkali and a bar that will chemically burn skin; this is the most consequential error in the craft. Measuring by volume rather than mass produces ratios that are wrong by an unpredictable margin because densities differ. Blending far too hot accelerates the reaction and can cause the batch to overheat, crack down the middle, or push a volcano of soap up out of the mould; blending far too cool produces false trace, where the mixture thickens because the solid fats are simply congealing rather than because an emulsion has formed, and it separates into layers in the mould. 

Ricing, where the batter breaks into grains resembling rice, and seizing, where it hardens to a solid mass within seconds, are almost always caused by a fragrance oil reacting with the alkaline batter. Neither is dangerous and neither is fixable in the moment; work fast, glop it into the mould, and accept an ugly bar that is chemically fine. Soda ash, the chalky white bloom that appears on exposed surfaces, is sodium carbonate formed when free alkali at the surface meets carbon dioxide in the air. It is cosmetic and harmless, and it planes off or steams away. 

For diagnosis after the fact, an oily film, weeping droplets, or a persistently soft bar generally means too much superfat or too little alkali. Such a bar is usually still safe and can often be rescued by remelting it with a correcting quantity of soap. A crumbly, brittle, chalky bar, particularly one that stings on contact, points the other way toward excess alkali, and that bar should be discarded rather than used or given away. When the two possibilities cannot be distinguished, treat the batch as caustic until a pH reading says otherwise.

sections.heading: Safety, Storage & Legal Notes
sections.body:
Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are corrosive substances, not merely irritants, and the distinction is mechanical. An alkali burn saponifies the fats in your own skin and denatures its proteins, so the injury liquefies tissue and keeps penetrating deeper for as long as the chemical remains in contact. Acid burns tend to coagulate tissue and self-limit; alkali burns do not. This is why an alkali splash on the eye is a genuine emergency capable of causing permanent corneal damage within minutes, and why a lye burn on skin is often painless at first, so the damage progresses before you notice it. A slippery, soapy feeling on the fingers is not a harmless sensation; it is your own skin being converted to soap. 

Lye also attacks metals. It reacts with aluminium, tin, and zinc, dissolving the metal and evolving hydrogen gas, which is flammable and, in a closed container, explosive. Never mix, store, or heat lye or raw soap batter in aluminium pans, foil, or unlined tins. Stainless steel, borosilicate glass, and heavy polypropylene or high-density polyethylene are the appropriate materials. 

The working rules are few and non-negotiable. Wear splash goggles, not spectacles, and chemical-resistant gloves for every step from opening the container to washing up. Work where air moves, and do not put your face over the vessel while the alkali dissolves, because the first minute produces a sharp aerosol that irritates the airway. Add lye to water, slowly, stirring, never the reverse. Keep children, pets, and food-preparation surfaces entirely out of the workspace, and label every container clearly, since a jar of clear lye solution on a shelf is indistinguishable from water. 

For skin contact, flush with copious cool running water for at least fifteen minutes and keep going if the slippery feeling persists. Do not pour vinegar over a substantial lye burn: neutralising a strong base with an acid is exothermic and adds a thermal injury to a chemical one. Dilute first, generously, with water. Vinegar's proper role is neutralising spills on benches and floors. Any eye contact, any burn larger than a coin, or any burn that blisters warrants medical assessment, and no written guide substitutes for that. 

Dry lye is hygroscopic and also absorbs carbon dioxide from the air, forming sodium carbonate, which both cakes the pellets and quietly weakens the product so that a recipe calculated on nominal purity under-doses. Keep it in an airtight container in a dry place and replace stock that has clumped solid. Finished soap wants the opposite of airtight: store bars somewhere dry with airflow, separated rather than stacked in plastic, so they continue hardening. Legally, making soap for your own household is unregulated almost everywhere, but selling it is not; cosmetic labelling, ingredient disclosure, safety assessment, and in some jurisdictions registration all apply the moment money changes hands, so check local rules before selling or even giving away at scale.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: Soapmaking is applied chemistry with real stakes, and the equipment list exists for three distinct reasons that are worth separating. The first is measurement precision: the reaction is stoichiometric, so the difference between a mild bar and a caustic one is a few grams, which no measuring cup can resolve. The second is chemical compatibility: a strong alkali attacks aluminium, tin, and zinc, dissolving the metal and releasing flammable hydrogen, so vessel material is a safety decision rather than a preference. The third is contamination in both directions, since anything that has touched raw lye should never return to food service, and food residues or tap-water minerals can discolour a batch or interfere with trace. Nothing here is exotic or expensive, and buying it once removes most of the ways a first batch goes wrong.
ingredients: A digital kitchen or postal scale, accurate to 1 gram (or better, 0.1 g for small batches) — soap is always measured by weight, never volume, because oils and lye solution have different densities; any inexpensive electronics or kitchen-supply scale works.

100% pure sodium hydroxide (lye), sold as pellets, flakes, or micro-beads — check the label reads only 'sodium hydroxide,' since some hardware-store drain cleaners blend in aluminum chips or other additives that will react violently and ruin a batch. Soapmaking suppliers and some hardware stores carry the pure form.

A dedicated heat-resistant mixing pitcher for the lye solution — heavy PP #5 plastic, Pyrex-type borosilicate glass, or stainless steel. Never aluminum, tin, or non-anodized metals; lye corrodes them and can release flammable hydrogen gas.
Chemical-splash goggles (not everyday glasses) and elbow-length chemical-resistant gloves (nitrile or heavy rubber), since a lye splash in the eye or on skin needs to be flushed immediately.
A well-ventilated space — outdoors, a garage with the door open, or a kitchen with the exhaust fan and windows on — because dissolving lye releases a sharp fume for the first minute or so.
A stick (immersion) blender kept exclusively for soap, never returned to food use once it's touched lye.
Heat-safe silicone or stainless spatulas and a silicone or lined mold, again dedicated to soapmaking.
Two thermometers (or one, rinsed between uses) — an instant-read digital or a candy thermometer works, one to track the lye solution and one for the melted oils.

Your chosen oils and fats (olive, coconut, palm or a palm-free substitute, shea or cocoa butter, lard, tallow, etc.), from a grocery store or bulk food supplier, and distilled water from the same, since tap-water minerals can discolor a batch or throw off trace.
A spray bottle of plain household vinegar kept within arm's reach — it neutralizes lye on skin or a spill on contact and buys you time before rinsing.
A reliable lye calculator (an online tool or a printed SAP-value chart) to check every batch's math independently before you weigh a single gram — never trust a recipe you haven't verified yourself.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Calculating and Pouring a Test Batch
sections.body: Saponification arithmetic only becomes intuitive once it has been run end to end on a batch small enough that an error costs 500 grams of oil rather than five kilograms. What follows is a complete worked example, a bar of 70 percent olive and 30 percent coconut oil at five percent superfat, carried from saponification values through lye and water weights to the physical pour. The blend is chosen because the two oils fail in opposite directions: olive alone gives a mild bar that stays soft for months and lathers thinly, while coconut alone gives a rock-hard bar that strips skin. Run the numbers yourself as you read rather than copying the results; independently verifying every batch's lye figure is the single practice that keeps the craft safe.
steps: Pick a total oil weight and a blend. For this test batch: 500 g total oil, split 350 g olive oil (70%) and 150 g coconut oil (30%) — a classic beginner combination that balances olive oil's mild, conditioning lather against coconut oil's hardness and big bubbles.

Look up each oil's NaOH SAP value from a reference chart: olive oil ≈ 0.134 g NaOH per gram of oil, coconut oil ≈ 0.183 g NaOH per gram. Treat these as approximate — always cross-check against a current chart or calculator, since published values vary slightly by source and by the oil's exact fatty-acid batch.

Multiply each oil weight by its SAP value: 350 g × 0.134 = 46.9 g NaOH for the olive oil; 150 g × 0.183 = 27.45 g NaOH for the coconut oil. Add them: 46.9 + 27.45 = 74.35 g of NaOH would saponify all the oil with zero fat left over.

Apply your superfat discount. At 5% superfat you deliberately leave 5% of the oil un-saponified for skin-conditioning excess fat, so you use only 95% of the calculated lye: 74.35 g × 0.95 ≈ 70.6 g NaOH — round to 70.6 g on the scale.

Decide your water amount via a lye concentration. A beginner-friendly choice is a 33% lye concentration (NaOH is 33% of the combined lye-solution weight), which works out close to the traditional 'water = 2× the lye weight' rule of thumb: 70.6 g × 2 ≈ 141 g of distilled water.
Put on goggles and gloves, and set up outdoors or by an open window. Weigh out 70.6 g of NaOH and 141 g of distilled water separately.

Always add lye to water, never water to lye — pouring water into concentrated lye can cause violent, sputtering boiling. Sprinkle the NaOH slowly into the water while stirring; the solution will fume briefly and can shoot up to 180–200°F (82–93°C) in under a minute from the heat of dissolution alone. Set it aside to cool, away from pets and kids.

Melt and combine your 350 g olive oil and 150 g coconut oil in a heat-safe pot, warming just enough to fully liquefy the coconut oil (its melting point is about 76°F/24°C), then let both the oils and the lye solution cool to roughly 100–110°F (38–43°C) — close enough that neither shocks the other on contact.

Pour the lye solution into the oils (not the reverse) and blend with the stick blender in short bursts, alternating with hand-stirring, until the mixture thickens to 'trace' — a state where a drizzle from the blender leaves a visible trail on the surface for a second or two before sinking back in.
Pour immediately into your mold, tap it firmly on the counter to release air bubbles, and cover. Leave it undisturbed 24–48 hours to fully set before unmolding and cutting into bars.

Cure the bars on a rack with airflow for 4–6 weeks, turning occasionally. This isn't just water evaporating — saponification itself keeps completing slowly over this period, and the bars get measurably milder and longer-lasting the longer they sit.

Before calling the batch good, do a zap test (touch a cut bar briefly to your tongue) — a genuine electric tingle means free lye is still present and the bar needs more cure time or was under-measured on the oil side; a soapy, faintly bitter taste with no zap means it's done.

sections.heading: Fatty Acid Profiles: Why Olive Oil Soap and Coconut Oil Soap Feel Nothing Alike
sections.body:
Every oil's behaviour in soap traces back to which fatty acids dominate its triglycerides, and each acid contributes a specific, well-characterised property to the finished bar. Lauric and myristic acids, the short twelve- and fourteen-carbon chains that make up well over 60 percent of coconut and babassu oil, saponify into unusually water-soluble salts that produce a big, fast, fluffy lather. That same solubility makes them aggressively cleansing: above roughly 25 to 30 percent of a recipe they strip the skin's own sebum and leave it tight and dry. Oleic acid, an eighteen-carbon monounsaturate that constitutes 65 to 80 percent of olive oil and dominates canola and high-oleic sunflower, gives the opposite: a soft, conditioning soap with a low, creamy lather and excellent mildness. That is precisely why a hundred percent olive oil Castile bar is famously gentle and famously slow, taking months rather than weeks to harden properly. 

Palmitic and stearic acids, the saturated sixteen- and eighteen-carbon chains dominant in palm oil, tallow, lard, and cocoa and shea butter, are the hardness contributors. They crystallise readily, producing a firm bar that survives a wet soap dish, and they generate a dense, stable, creamy lather rather than large bubbles. A well-balanced bar generally wants some of all three families: enough lauric for a lather that appears quickly, enough palmitic and stearic for structure, and a majority of oleic for mildness. 

Linoleic and linolenic acids, the polyunsaturates found in soybean, sunflower, grapeseed, and hemp oil, condition beautifully but carry a real cost. Their multiple carbon-carbon double bonds are vulnerable to atmospheric oxidation, and the oxidation products appear on a cured bar as dreaded orange spots, rust-coloured blotches accompanied by a stale crayon smell that can develop months after the bar seemed finished. Keeping high-linoleic oils to a modest fraction of a recipe, and using fresh rather than long-stored oils, is the practical control. 

Soapmakers quantify this oxidative exposure with the iodine value, a laboratory measure of how much iodine a fat absorbs and therefore how many double bonds it contains. Higher iodine value means more unsaturation, a softer bar, and a shorter shelf life; keeping a blend's overall iodine value below about 70 tends to give a bar that stores well for a year or more. The chemist and soap researcher Kevin Dunn popularised combining saponification value and iodine value into a single INS number, roughly the SAP value minus the iodine value, as a quick balance check. Blends landing somewhere around 150 to 170 tend to produce bars that are neither too soft, as olive-heavy low-INS recipes are, nor too hard and drying, as an all-coconut or all-palm high-INS recipe is. It is worth treating INS as a rough orientation rather than a target, since it says nothing about which specific acids produced the number, and two very different blends can share an INS and feel nothing alike. Making and using the bar remains the only real test.

sections.heading: The Gel Phase: Heat, Color, and Why Some Soaps Turn Translucent
sections.body:
Making soap involves two entirely separate heat events, and confusing them is a common source of misunderstanding. The first is purely physical and happens the instant sodium hydroxide meets water. Dissolving NaOH releases on the order of 44 kilojoules per mole as its crystal lattice breaks apart and the ions hydrate, which is enough to drive a concentrated lye solution from room temperature to somewhere between 82 and 93 °C in under a minute. No oil has reacted at this point; this is dissolution alone, and it is the reason the mixing vessel must be heat-resistant and the reason the solution needs twenty to forty minutes of cooling before it meets the fats. 

The second heat event is the saponification reaction itself, which is also exothermic but far more gradual, unfolding over hours inside the mould as the ester bonds break. Whether that heat is retained or allowed to escape determines the bar's appearance. Insulate a freshly poured mould, by wrapping it in towels or setting it in an oven with only the light on, and the centre can climb past 65 to 77 °C and enter what soapmakers call gel phase. The soap turns glossy, translucent, and noticeably darker, and the transition spreads outward from the centre as a visible front over several hours before the batch cools back to an opaque matte finish. 

Gel is not a chemical requirement, but it has consequences. A gelled batch saponifies faster and more completely, can often be unmoulded and cut sooner, and typically shows brighter, more saturated colour, because the elevated temperature helps pigments disperse and prevents the mottled patches that appear when a colourant sets unevenly in a cool batch. Gelled soap also tends to be marginally harder at any given age. 

Preventing gel is an equally legitimate choice, achieved by pouring into a mould placed in the refrigerator or freezer for the first day, or simply leaving it uncovered in a cool room. The result is a fully opaque bar with soft, pastel colouring throughout. This is standard practice for milk soaps, and for a specific chemical reason: the lactose in goat's milk and the sugars in coconut milk caramelise and then scorch at gel temperatures, turning the batch orange-brown and developing an unpleasant burnt, ammoniacal smell that no amount of curing removes. Honey, beer, and fruit purée additions carry the same risk for the same reason, since all of them contribute fermentable sugars that accelerate the reaction and raise the peak temperature. 

Neither route is right or wrong. It is an aesthetic and formulation decision rather than a safety one, provided the batch was measured correctly to begin with. The genuinely undesirable outcome is the partial gel: an unevenly insulated mould where the warm centre gels and the cool edges do not, leaving a translucent core ringed by an opaque border. It is harmless, and it is the reason soapmakers tend to commit firmly to one approach rather than leaving a mould half-covered.

sections.heading: Hot Process Soapmaking and Rebatching a Failed Batch
sections.body:
Cold process lets saponification finish slowly at room temperature over the following weeks. Hot process instead applies external heat, from a slow cooker on low or a double boiler, to drive the same reaction to near-completion in a couple of hours inside the pot. The chemistry is identical; only the rate changes, since raising the temperature increases the frequency and energy of molecular collisions and so speeds the breaking of the ester bonds. After reaching trace, the batch is cooked for roughly 45 minutes to an hour, and it passes through a sequence of visible stages that serve as a progress indicator: it first bubbles and puffs up at the edges, then folds in on itself, then turns glossy and translucent in what is universally called the vaseline stage, and finally thickens into an opaque, waxy, mashed-potato consistency that is spooned rather than poured into the mould. 

The payoff is that hot-process soap is technically safe to use as soon as it has cooled and hardened, because the alkali has already been consumed in the pot rather than in the mould. In practice a short cure of one to two weeks still repays itself: water continues evaporating, and a drier bar is harder and lasts substantially longer in use. Hot process also tolerates additives that cold process punishes. Fragrance oils, botanicals, and delicate ingredients are stirred in after the cook, when the batter is no longer strongly alkaline, so they neither seize the batch nor discolour over weeks of ongoing chemistry, and a chosen superfat oil added at this stage genuinely remains as that oil rather than being consumed. The trade-offs are cosmetic: hot-process soap has a rustic, textured surface and cannot hold the fine swirls and layered pours that cold process allows, because the batter is a thick paste by the time it enters the mould. 

Rebatching is the craft's repair procedure. Soap that separated, went grainy, seized before fragrance could be added, or simply came out ugly is grated or chopped into small pieces, returned to a double boiler or slow cooker with a modest splash of water, milk, or extra oil, and warmed gently until it can be stirred into a smooth, cohesive mass and pressed back into a mould. Low, slow heat matters here, since direct high heat will scorch the sugars and darken the batch. 

The critical limit is worth stating plainly. Rebatching fixes mechanical and cosmetic failures, emulsion problems, separation, and appearance. It cannot fix a miscalculated recipe. If the original alkali weight was wrong, the excess or deficit is already locked into the chemistry, and remelting changes nothing about the ratio of alkali to fat. A lye-heavy batch can in principle be corrected by rebatching it together with a calculated quantity of a heavily superfatted batch, but that requires knowing the original error precisely, which is rarely the case. A bar that zaps or reads above pH 11 after a rebatch should be discarded. The fix for bad arithmetic always belongs at the calculation stage, not the stove.

sections.heading: First Principles: Disinfection vs Purification
sections.body:
Disinfection means killing or inactivating the microorganisms that cause disease: bacteria, viruses, and protozoa. It is emphatically not the same thing as making water chemically pure. A disinfectant attacks living or infectious agents and does nothing whatsoever about dissolved lead, arsenic, nitrate, pesticide residue, road salt, or industrial solvent. Water from a stream below a mine can be perfectly disinfected and still poison you. Keeping these two problems separate is the first and most consequential distinction in the subject, because the failure mode is silent: chlorinated contaminated water tastes treated. 

A handful of terms carry most of the working knowledge. A pathogen is simply a microbe capable of causing disease. The CT value is the product of disinfectant concentration, measured in milligrams per litre, which is numerically the same as parts per million, multiplied by contact time in minutes, so CT equals C times t. Because a given degree of kill requires a minimum CT, the two variables trade against each other: half the concentration demands twice the time, and vice versa. This single relationship is why every dosing instruction comes paired with a waiting period, and why shortening the wait quietly undoes the dose. 

Residual is the disinfectant still present after everything reactive in the water has been satisfied. It matters twice over: it is the evidence you added enough, and it keeps protecting the water against recontamination during storage. A free chlorine residual of roughly 0.2 to 0.5 milligrams per litre is the common target for stored drinking water. Turbidity is cloudiness caused by suspended particles, and it is the most underrated enemy of chemical treatment. Particles physically shield microbes from the disinfectant and, being largely organic, consume it directly. Always settle or pre-filter cloudy water before treating it, and double the dose for water that remains cloudy or is very cold. 

Both chlorine and iodine work by oxidation. They are electron-hungry molecules that attack cell membranes, disrupt enzyme systems, and damage nucleic acids, destroying the microbe's ability to function rather than merely inhibiting it. That mechanism explains their one shared blind spot. Cryptosporidium, a protozoan parasite, forms an oocyst with a tough multi-layered wall that oxidants penetrate extremely slowly, and neither chlorine nor iodine kills it reliably at any dose a person would willingly drink. Giardia cysts are also resistant, though less extremely so. Against Cryptosporidium, the answer is physical: boiling, or filtration through an absolute one-micron or finer barrier. Knowing which pathogens your chosen method does not cover is as important as knowing the dose. 

One further term is worth defining because dosing guidance depends on it. Log reduction expresses kill as powers of ten: a 1-log reduction removes 90 percent of the organisms present, 2-log removes 99 percent, 3-log 99.9 percent, and 4-log 99.99 percent. Targets are stated this way because no practical process reduces a population to literally zero, and because starting concentration matters. Water carrying millions of organisms per litre can still hold thousands after a 3-log reduction, which argues for choosing the cleanest available source rather than relying on chemistry to rescue the worst one.

sections.heading: Chlorine Chemistry and Free vs Combined Chlorine
sections.body:
When chlorine is added to water as sodium hypochlorite bleach, it does not remain as the compound you poured in. It hydrolyses, producing hypochlorous acid and hypochlorite ion: NaOCl plus H₂O gives HOCl plus Na⁺ plus OH⁻, and the hypochlorous acid then sits in equilibrium with its dissociated form, HOCl in balance with H⁺ plus OCl⁻. That these two species coexist, and are not equally useful, explains most of chlorine's practical behaviour. 

Hypochlorous acid is the effective germ-killer, commonly cited as somewhere between 40 and 100 times more potent than hypochlorite ion. The reason is electrostatic. HOCl is a small, electrically neutral molecule, so it diffuses through a microbial cell membrane readily and attacks the machinery inside. OCl⁻ carries a negative charge, and the cell surface is also negatively charged, so it is repelled and must do its work from outside. Same element, same test-strip reading, radically different killing power. 

Which of the two dominates is set almost entirely by pH, the measure of acidity defined as the negative base-ten logarithm of the hydrogen-ion concentration, running 0 to 14 with 7 as neutral. The changeover point, the pKa of hypochlorous acid, sits near 7.5. At pH 6 to 7, roughly 75 to 96 percent of the free chlorine exists as active HOCl and disinfection is strong. By pH 8 and above, most has converted to the feeble OCl⁻ and killing power falls sharply even though the measured chlorine concentration has not changed at all. Slightly acidic to neutral water therefore disinfects far better than alkaline water at the same dose. 

Two further terms complete the picture. Free chlorine is the sum of HOCl and OCl⁻, meaning the chlorine still available to kill things. Combined chlorine is chlorine that has already reacted with ammonia or organic nitrogen to form chloramines, which are far weaker disinfectants, act much more slowly, and are responsible for the harsh smell people mistakenly attribute to over-chlorination. Total chlorine is the two added together, which is why a test kit that reads only total chlorine can reassure you about water that has almost no active disinfectant left in it. 

The transition between those two regimes has a name worth knowing. As chlorine is added to water containing ammonia, it is consumed forming chloramines and the free chlorine reading stays near zero; only once enough has been added to oxidise those chloramines away, a threshold water engineers call the breakpoint, does free chlorine begin to accumulate. The practical implication is unforgiving: under-dosing such water does not deliver partial disinfection so much as almost none, because everything added went into forming weak combined chlorine instead. 

Chlorine demand is the quantity consumed by reacting with everything else present before any residual can accumulate: organic matter, iron, manganese, sulphide, ammonia. Dirty water eats chlorine, and it eats it first. This is why a dose that works perfectly on clear tap water may leave zero residual in silty pond water, and why the presence of a measurable residual after the contact time is the only real proof that the demand was met and the disinfection actually happened.

sections.heading: Exact Bleach Doses for Drinking Water
sections.body:
Ordinary unscented household bleach is a solution of sodium hypochlorite, and the first thing to do is read the label, because the concentration is not standardised. Commonly sold strengths include 5, 6, 7.5, and 8.25 percent available chlorine, a spread wide enough that a dose correct for one is meaningfully wrong for another. Use only plain bleach. Scented products, splash-less or thickened formulations, and anything blended with detergents or other cleaners contain additives that are not meant for ingestion and that also alter the effective chlorine content. 

The emergency drinking-water guidance published by public-health agencies, expressed for roughly 6 percent bleach, is straightforward. For clear water, add 2 drops per litre, which is about 8 drops per US gallon. For cloudy or cold water, double it to 4 drops per litre, about 16 per gallon, and pre-filter through a cloth or coffee filter first. A useful volumetric equivalent is that one eighth of a teaspoon, roughly 8 drops, treats about 4 litres of clear water. For 8.25 percent bleach, use close to half again less per volume, on the order of 2 drops per 2 litres, because the stronger product delivers more chlorine per drop. 

The procedure has four parts, and the order matters. Clarify first: filter cloudy water through cloth and let sediment settle, because suspended solids both shield microbes and consume chlorine before it can reach them. Add the counted drops and stir thoroughly for around thirty seconds so the chlorine disperses rather than sitting near the surface. Let it stand for 30 minutes of contact time, and extend that substantially in cold water, since the reaction slows markedly below about 10 degrees Celsius; doubling the wait to an hour is the standard field adjustment. 

Then check by smell, which is the field test available when no test kit is. Correctly treated water carries a faint, clean chlorine odour, comparable to a lightly chlorinated swimming pool. If there is no chlorine smell at all, the demand exceeded the dose and the water was probably not disinfected; repeat the dose and wait another 15 to 30 minutes. If a second dose still leaves no detectable chlorine, discard that water and find another source, because the organic load is high enough that you cannot know what happened chemically. An overwhelming bleach smell means you overshot, which is unpleasant but not usually hazardous at these dilutions; letting it stand open for a while allows it to dissipate. 

As a worked example, suppose you have a 10-litre jug of clear water and 6 percent bleach. The dose is 2 drops per litre times 10 litres, so 20 drops, roughly a quarter teaspoon. Stir, cover, wait 30 minutes at ordinary temperature or 60 minutes if the water is near freezing, and the result is drinkable water carrying a faint protective chlorine residual for storage.

sections.heading: Iodine Dosing and Its Limits
sections.body:
Iodine is an effective alternative oxidant and is particularly convenient for travel, since tablets are light, compact, and unaffected by the freezing that ruptures some filter cartridges. Working doses for one litre of clear water depend on the form. Iodine tablets, generally tetraglycine hydroperiodide sold under names such as Potable Aqua, are typically one tablet per litre, doubled to two for cloudy or cold water. Two percent tincture of iodine, the familiar brown antiseptic bottle, takes 5 drops per litre of clear water and 10 drops if cloudy. Stronger preparations such as five percent Lugol's solution take proportionally fewer, roughly 2 drops per litre. In every case the product's own instructions supersede a general table, because concentration and formulation vary. Standard contact time is 30 minutes, but that figure assumes reasonably warm water; at around 5 degrees Celsius, extend it to 60 minutes or more, since the oxidation reaction slows with temperature just as chlorine's does. 

The limits deserve as much attention as the doses. Iodine is not suitable for prolonged use. Beyond a few weeks of continuous consumption it can disturb thyroid function, because the thyroid actively concentrates iodine to make its hormones and both excess and deficiency disrupt that system. It should not be used at all by anyone who is pregnant, who has a thyroid disorder, or who has a known iodine sensitivity; the frequently repeated shellfish-allergy connection is now regarded as a myth in allergy medicine, but a genuine reaction to topical iodine antiseptics is a real contraindication. Anyone in those categories should take medical advice rather than relying on a general guide, and nothing written here substitutes for that. 

Like chlorine, iodine does not reliably inactivate Cryptosporidium. The oocyst wall resists oxidants sufficiently that no practical dose and wait will do the job, so agricultural runoff, water downstream of livestock, and any source with a known Crypto risk needs boiling or a filter rated to remove cysts instead. Giardia is killed but slowly, which is another reason the contact time is not negotiable. 

Iodine also leaves a distinct medicinal taste and a yellow-brown tint, which is the most common reason people abandon it. A very small pinch of ascorbic acid, ordinary vitamin C, chemically reduces the residual iodine to colourless, tasteless iodide and clears both problems within seconds. The timing is critical and frequently botched: add it only after the full contact time has elapsed. Adding vitamin C at the start destroys the iodine's oxidising power immediately and leaves you with untreated water that looks and tastes reassuringly clean. Many tablet products sell a second bottle of neutraliser tablets for exactly this purpose, and their instructions are explicit about the sequence for the same reason.

sections.heading: Making a Safe Surface Sanitizer
sections.body:
Sanitising a hard surface uses a much stronger chlorine solution than drinking water does, and the solution is left to work wet rather than wiped off immediately. The reason for the higher concentration is that a surface carries a heavy organic load and the contact time available is minutes rather than half an hour, so the CT relationship is satisfied by pushing the concentration up instead. This solution is not drinkable at any point. 

For general household surfaces, roughly one tablespoon of 6 percent bleach in one US gallon, about 4 litres, of room-temperature water gives approximately 200 parts per million free chlorine, which is the standard food-contact sanitising strength. For disinfecting after known contamination, vomit, faeces, or a sickroom, a third of a cup per gallon gives something near 1,900 parts per million, appropriate for heavy jobs and correspondingly harsher on surfaces, fabrics, and lungs. 

Cleaning must come before sanitising, and this is the step most often skipped. Visible soil, grease, and food residue consume chlorine directly through the same demand reaction that operates in water, so applying sanitiser to a dirty surface may exhaust it before it touches a single microbe. Wash with detergent, rinse, then apply the chlorine solution and keep the surface visibly wet for the required dwell time. That time ranges from about 1 minute for easy targets up to 10 minutes for resistant ones, with roughly 5 minutes a defensible default. Surfaces that will touch food should be rinsed with clean water afterwards; others can simply air-dry. 

Four safety rules are non-negotiable. Never mix bleach with ammonia, which is present in many glass and floor cleaners: the reaction releases chloramine vapours that cause severe airway injury. Never mix bleach with acids, including vinegar, toilet-bowl cleaners, and limescale removers, because that liberates chlorine gas directly. Bleach solutions degrade, losing strength through decomposition accelerated by light, heat, and dilution, so mix fresh, use within 24 hours, and store the concentrate cool and dark. And ventilate the space and wear gloves, since chlorine at working strength irritates skin, eyes, and the respiratory tract. 

Alcohol is a useful alternative with entirely different chemistry: it kills by denaturing proteins and dissolving lipid membranes rather than by oxidation. A solution of 60 to 70 percent ethanol or isopropanol by volume is highly effective on surfaces and hands. Both boundaries matter. Below about 60 percent the concentration is too weak to denature proteins reliably, and above roughly 80 percent it becomes counterproductive, because a small proportion of water is needed to carry the alcohol into the cell and to slow evaporation enough for the contact to happen at all. Pure alcohol evaporates before it works. Alcohol also does not kill bacterial spores and performs poorly on visibly soiled surfaces, and its vapour is flammable, so keep it well away from flame and hot elements.

sections.heading: Physical Backup Methods & When Chemistry Fails
sections.body:
Chemistry has real limits, and knowing the physical fallbacks is what keeps a treatment plan honest. Boiling is the most reliable single method available against pathogens, and unlike chlorine and iodine it handles Cryptosporidium and Giardia without difficulty, because heat denatures proteins throughout the organism regardless of how tough its outer wall is. A rolling boil held for one full minute inactivates essentially every waterborne pathogen of concern. Above roughly 2,000 metres, about 6,500 feet, extend that to three minutes: reduced atmospheric pressure lowers water's boiling point to around 93 degrees Celsius at that altitude compared with 100 at sea level, so the same thermal kill needs longer. Boiling does nothing about dissolved chemicals, salts, or heavy metals, and by driving off water it actually concentrates them slightly. 

Solar disinfection, universally shortened to SODIS, uses a clear PET plastic or glass bottle laid in direct sun for six hours, or two consecutive days if the sky is overcast. Ultraviolet-A radiation damages microbial DNA while mild heating adds a synergistic effect, and the World Health Organization endorses it as an emergency option. It requires genuinely clear water, since turbidity blocks ultraviolet penetration within centimetres, and it removes no chemical contamination and leaves no protective residual. 

Filtration works mechanically. A filter with an absolute rating of one micron or finer physically excludes protozoan cysts including Cryptosporidium and Giardia, and removes most bacteria. Viruses are the exception: at roughly 0.02 to 0.3 microns they pass straight through a cyst-rated filter, so only devices specifically certified for virus removal, or a filter paired with a chemical step, address them. Note also the difference between an absolute and a nominal rating, since a nominal one micron filter may pass a meaningful fraction of one-micron particles. 

The decision logic follows from these limits. Cloudy water is always filtered or settled first, whatever comes next. Suspected chemical or industrial contamination is not helped at all by chlorine or iodine, and calls for distillation, activated carbon plus a specific treatment, or simply a different source; this is the case where a confident chemical dose gives dangerous false assurance. Suspected Cryptosporidium, which agricultural runoff and livestock catchments should always raise, means boiling or filtering rather than relying on oxidants. When there is neither fuel nor chemical available, SODIS is the fallback. 

The strongest practical approach combines methods, because their weaknesses are complementary: filter to remove cysts and turbidity, then chlorinate to kill viruses and bacteria and leave a residual. Whatever the route, store treated water in clean covered containers, since recontamination from a dirty jug or unwashed hands undoes the entire process, and maintaining a small chlorine residual is what protects water sitting in storage for days.

sections.heading: Equipment for Testing and Treating Water Yourself
sections.body:
Doing your own dosing and verification, rather than trusting a printed chart, takes a small, inexpensive kit, and each item closes a specific gap in what a chart can tell you. The central problem is that published dose tables assume a set of conditions — clear water near room temperature at roughly neutral pH — and real water rarely matches all three. Each measurement reveals how far your water departs from those assumptions. 

Concentration is the first unknown. Bleach degrades in storage, losing perhaps a fifth of its available chlorine over a year at room temperature and more if kept warm or in light, so an old bottle labelled 6 percent may deliver closer to 4. Only a test kit reading free chlorine — not total, which includes spent chloramines — tells you what actually arrived in the water. 

Temperature and pH quietly change the answer without changing the dose. Cold slows the oxidation reaction, so the same concentration needs a longer wait; alkaline water shifts the chlorine equilibrium toward the weak hypochlorite ion, so the same reading does less work. A thermometer and a pH test turn both into numbers you can respond to. 

The rest address precision. A dropper or graduated syringe makes a small dose repeatable rather than approximate, containers of known volume map the arithmetic onto real water, a timer stops you guessing at contact time, and a cloth or coffee filter handles turbidity — not an optional refinement but the largest single source of treatment failure. Gloves matter because concentrated bleach and iodine tincture irritate skin with repeated handling.
ingredients: Plain, unscented household bleach labeled as sodium hypochlorite solution (typically 5–9% available chlorine), with no added fragrance, colorants, or 'splash-less' thickeners — those additives change the effective concentration and complicate dosing. Any grocery or hardware store carries a plain version.
A liquid medicine dropper or oral dosing syringe graduated in mL or drops, for precise small-volume dosing — pharmacies sell these cheaply, often free with liquid medication.
A chlorine test kit — either DPD drop-based or test strips, sold at pool-supply and hardware stores — that reads free and total chlorine in the 0–10 ppm range.
A pH test kit or digital pH meter/strips, also from a pool-supply or aquarium store, since chlorine's effectiveness depends heavily on the water's pH.
A 2% tincture of iodine bottle with its own built-in dropper, from a pharmacy, if you want to practice the iodine dosing method as well.
Clear glass or food-grade plastic containers of a known volume (1-liter measuring pitchers work well) so your dose calculations map directly onto a real quantity of water.
A basic liquid thermometer, since cold water needs longer contact times than the tables often assume.
A stopwatch or a phone timer, to hold yourself to the actual contact time rather than guessing.
Nitrile gloves, since concentrated bleach and iodine tincture will irritate skin with repeated contact.

A coffee filter, clean cotton cloth, or fine paper towel for pre-filtering cloudy water — chlorine and iodine both work far worse in turbid water, so clarifying first is part of the real procedure, not an afterthought.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Dosing, Timing and Verifying a Batch of Water
sections.body: Dosing arithmetic stops being abstract the moment you run it on a real litre of water and measure whether it worked. Treating one measured litre, timing the contact period properly, and verifying with a test kit rather than assuming success is the fastest way to discover that your water is not the idealised water the tables assume. Three checks carry most of the value: the smell test, the only verification available in the field with no equipment; the free chlorine residual, the evidence that enough disinfectant survived the water's demand; and the pH reading, which explains an adequate-looking residual that nonetheless disinfects weakly. Work with water you are willing to discard.
steps: Draw exactly 1 liter of the water you intend to treat into a clear container. If it's visibly cloudy or has floating sediment, pre-filter it through a clean cloth or coffee filter first — disinfectant demand rises sharply in turbid water because chlorine reacts with suspended organic matter before it ever reaches a pathogen.
Check the bleach bottle's label for its percentage of available chlorine (commonly 6% for standard household bleach in most markets, sometimes 5% or 8.25%).

Using the dosing formula from the earlier section for 6% bleach, calculate the number of drops needed for 1 liter at a standard treatment target (roughly 2 drops of 6% bleach per liter for clear water, doubled to about 4 drops for cloudy water) — write the number down before you add anything.

Add the calculated number of drops with your dropper, counting out loud, then stir or shake the container thoroughly for about 30 seconds so the chlorine disperses evenly rather than pooling near the surface.

Check your water's temperature. If it's below about 10°C (50°F), extend the standard 30-minute contact time — cold slows the disinfection reaction considerably, and doubling the wait to 60 minutes is a reasonable field adjustment.
Start your timer and let the water stand, covered, for the full contact time — do not drink or taste it during this window.

At the end of the wait, smell the water: a faint, clean chlorine odor (like a lightly chlorinated pool) is the sign you dosed correctly. No smell at all suggests you under-dosed or the chlorine was consumed by contaminants; an overpowering bleach smell means you over-dosed.

Use your test kit to measure the free chlorine residual. A properly treated batch should read roughly 0.2–0.5 ppm free chlorine remaining after the contact time — this residual is your proof that enough chlorine survived contact with everything in the water to still be actively protecting it.

Check the pH strip or meter reading. If it's above about 8, note that your effective disinfection was weaker than the same dose at neutral pH (see below) — repeat the test at a slightly higher dose and compare the residual.

Repeat the whole test once using deliberately cloudy water (stir in a pinch of dirt) without pre-filtering, and once after filtering it — comparing the two final chlorine residuals is the clearest hands-on demonstration of why clarifying water before treating it matters as much as the dose itself.

sections.heading: Contact Time, CT Values, and Why Cold Water Needs More of Both
sections.body:
Disinfection efficacy is not governed by how much chlorine you add alone, but by the product of concentration and time, the quantity water engineers call the CT value: concentration in milligrams per litre multiplied by contact time in minutes, giving units of milligram-minutes per litre. A given CT achieves a specific log reduction of a specific organism, where each log represents a tenfold decrease, so 3-log means 99.9 percent inactivation and 4-log means 99.99 percent. Because the two factors multiply, halving the concentration and doubling the time is, to a first approximation, the same treatment. 

Different organisms demand wildly different CTs, and this is the fact that makes a single universal dose impossible. Ordinary enteric bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella, along with most enveloped viruses, fall quickly to free chlorine, often needing a CT of only a few milligram-minutes per litre for 3-log reduction. Non-enveloped viruses like hepatitis A and norovirus need considerably more. Giardia cysts are tougher again: regulatory treatment tables put the CT for 3-log Giardia inactivation somewhere in the region of 100 or more milligram-minutes per litre at near-freezing water and neutral pH. That number is precisely where the familiar field rule comes from. Holding 1 to 2 parts per million of free chlorine for 30 minutes yields a CT of 30 to 60, which sits in the right range for warmer water and explains why the guidance pairs a modest dose with a wait that feels disproportionately long. 

Cryptosporidium sits outside this scheme entirely. Its oocyst wall is so resistant that the CT required for meaningful inactivation by free chlorine runs into the thousands of milligram-minutes per litre, which would mean either a dose far past the point of palatability or a wait measured in many hours. That is not a marginal shortfall to be closed by adding a few more drops; it is a categorical failure of the method, and it is the whole reason boiling or filtration is the recommended defence against Crypto rather than any amount of household bleach. 

Temperature is the other lever, and it is systematically underestimated. Chemical reaction rates fall as temperature drops, roughly following the rule that a 10-degree Celsius decrease halves the rate for many reactions, so the CT required at 0.5 degrees can be three to four times that required at 25 degrees for the same kill. A walker treating snowmelt at 3 degrees with the drop count printed for clear water is therefore under-treating relative to a summer stream at 20 degrees unless something changes. The right correction is to extend the contact time rather than increase the dose, because chlorine passes the taste threshold well before it meaningfully raises the CT, and an undrinkably chlorinated bottle that gets poured out protects nobody.

sections.heading: pH's Hidden Role: Why Chlorine Stops Working in Alkaline Water
sections.body:
Free chlorine in water does not exist as a single substance. It partitions between hypochlorous acid, HOCl, and the hypochlorite ion, OCl⁻, and the ratio between them is controlled almost entirely by pH through the equilibrium HOCl in balance with H⁺ plus OCl⁻, whose pKa sits at approximately 7.5. The pKa is simply the pH at which the two forms are present in equal amounts, so it functions as the tipping point of the whole system. 

The distinction matters because the two species are not remotely equal as disinfectants. Hypochlorous acid is commonly cited as 40 to 80 times more effective at inactivating microorganisms, and the reason is physical rather than chemical. HOCl is electrically neutral and small, so it diffuses through a microbial cell envelope and reaches the enzymes and nucleic acids inside. OCl⁻ carries a negative charge, and since bacterial surfaces are also negatively charged, electrostatic repulsion keeps it largely outside the cell where it can only attack the surface. 

The numbers follow the equilibrium sharply. At pH 6, over 95 percent of the free chlorine present is in the active HOCl form. At pH 7.5, by definition, the split is about even. By pH 8.5, the balance has swung hard toward the weak OCl⁻ and perhaps a tenth of the chlorine remains in the potent form. The critical and counterintuitive consequence is that a test strip reading 2 parts per million of free chlorine at pH 8.5 represents dramatically less killing power than the identical reading at pH 7, even though the instrument reports the same number. The measurement is not wrong; it simply does not measure the thing that matters. 

This is exactly why pool operators are instructed to hold pH between roughly 7.2 and 7.6. The reason is not bather comfort alone. Letting pH drift upward silently wastes chlorine's disinfecting capacity while every readable number on the test kit continues to look correct, which is a particularly dangerous kind of failure because it is invisible to routine monitoring. 

For treating drinking water with household bleach, the standard drop-count guidance implicitly assumes roughly neutral source water. Naturally alkaline supplies, which are common in limestone and chalk regions and in any water that has had lime or soda ash added for corrosion control upstream, can easily sit at pH 8 or above. Such water should either be dosed higher or given a substantially longer contact time to reach the same CT. There is a further subtlety worth knowing: adding hypochlorite bleach itself raises pH slightly, because the hydrolysis reaction releases hydroxide, so heavy dosing of poorly buffered water can push it in the unhelpful direction. If you are testing pH at all, treating at pH 7 rather than pH 8 buys a materially larger safety margin for exactly the same quantity of bleach and exactly the same wait.

sections.heading: Beyond Chlorine and Iodine: Chlorine Dioxide, Ozone, and Solar Disinfection
sections.body:
Household bleach and iodine tincture dominate practical water treatment because they are cheap, shelf-stable, and dosed with arithmetic simple enough to do in the field, but they are not the only chemistries available, and each alternative trades differently. 

Chlorine dioxide, ClO₂, is sold as two-part liquid drops that are mixed to generate the gas in solution, or as effervescent tablets that do the same. Chemically it is a distinct compound rather than a form of chlorine, and it works by electron transfer rather than by chlorination, which has two useful consequences: it does not depend on the HOCl and OCl⁻ equilibrium and therefore stays effective across a much wider pH range, and it is markedly better than chlorine at inactivating Cryptosporidium. It also produces far fewer chlorinated disinfection by-products and leaves less taste. The important caveat is that even chlorine dioxide is slow against Crypto: commercial products commonly specify a four-hour wait for that organism against 30 minutes for bacteria and viruses, so read the actual instructions rather than assuming one contact time covers everything. It is also less shelf-stable once activated and more expensive per litre treated. 

Ozone, O₃, is a stronger oxidiser than any chlorine species and is used widely in municipal treatment works and bottled-water plants, where it inactivates Cryptosporidium at practical doses and leaves no taste. Its disqualifying property for personal use is that it provides no residual whatsoever: ozone decomposes back to ordinary oxygen within minutes, with a half-life in water of roughly 20 to 30 minutes at room temperature and shorter when warm. It must therefore be generated electrically on demand and used immediately, which means equipment and power, and treated water has no ongoing protection against recontamination in storage. 

Solar water disinfection is the simplest non-chemical route. Filling clear PET plastic bottles, ideally no more than two or three litres so ultraviolet light penetrates the full depth, and leaving them in direct unobstructed sunlight for six hours, or two consecutive days under cloud, combines UV-A damage to microbial DNA with mild thermal stress. The World Health Organization endorses it as an emergency measure. Its limits are strict: it needs genuinely clear water, since turbidity blocks ultraviolet within a short distance, it requires real sun rather than a bright overcast, and like ozone it leaves no residual, so water can be recontaminated the instant it is decanted into a dirty container. Laying bottles on a reflective surface such as corrugated iron improves both the heating and the effective dose. 

None of these methods removes the judgement involved in choosing one. They are additional tools for the situations where chlorine's pH sensitivity, iodine's thyroid caveats, or a simple shortage of available contact time make a primary method a poor fit for the water actually in front of you.

guides.title: Distillation, Extraction & Purifying Liquids
guides.summary: The physics of separating and purifying liquids: distillation and boiling points, condensation, solvent extraction, filtration, and building a simple still — with worked temperatures and safety.

sections.heading: Core Principles: Why Liquids Separate
sections.body:
Every method of purifying or separating a liquid exploits the fact that different substances hold on to one another with different strengths. The single most useful number is the boiling point: the temperature at which a liquid's vapour pressure equals the pressure of the atmosphere pressing down on it, so that vapour bubbles can form throughout the body of the liquid rather than molecules merely escaping from its surface. Water boils at 100 °C at sea level under 101.3 kilopascals; ethanol boils at 78.4 °C; acetone at 56 °C; and ordinary table salt does not boil at any temperature a kitchen can reach — it simply stays behind, dissolved in whatever water remains. Because the definition depends on the surrounding pressure, boiling point is not a fixed property of a substance but a property of a substance at a stated pressure. Water boils near 95 °C at 1,600 metres of elevation and near 70 °C on the summit of Everest, which is why food cooks slowly at altitude and why a distillation run high in the mountains settles at a lower thermometer reading than the textbook value.

Vapour pressure is the quantity underneath all of this. It is the pressure exerted by molecules escaping a liquid surface into the space above it, and it climbs steeply with temperature. A substance with a high vapour pressure at room temperature is called volatile: it evaporates readily, tends to smell strongly, and will come over first in a distillation. Condensation is simply the reverse — cooling a vapour until its molecules no longer carry enough energy to remain in the gas phase, so they return to liquid.

Solubility governs extraction rather than distillation. It measures how much of one substance will dissolve in another, and the working rule is that like dissolves like. Water is a polar molecule with an uneven distribution of charge, so it dissolves other polar and ionic substances well: salt, sugar, many acids. Oils and fats are non-polar and dissolve in non-polar solvents such as hexane, and partly in ethanol, which is unusual in carrying both a polar hydroxyl group and a non-polar carbon tail and so straddles both worlds. That dual character is exactly why ethanol extracts plant compounds plain water cannot touch.

Two liquids that mix in all proportions, such as water and ethanol, are miscible. Two that refuse and settle into distinct layers, such as oil and water, are immiscible, and that refusal is itself a separation technique: let the mixture settle in a vessel with a tap at the base and draw the lower layer off. Distillation combines all of these ideas. Heat a mixture, the more volatile component enriches in the vapour, and if that vapour is led away and cooled elsewhere it condenses as a liquid purer than the pot it came from. Anything with no meaningful vapour pressure — salt, minerals, heavy metals, bacteria — is simply left behind.

sections.heading: Simple Distillation: Building a Basic Still
sections.body:
A still, however elaborate, has only three functional parts. The first is a boiling vessel, heated and holding the mixture to be separated. The second is a condenser: a length of tube kept cold, where vapour gives up its latent heat and returns to liquid. The third is a receiver, a clean vessel that catches the distillate. Everything else — thermometers, packed columns, ground-glass joints, water jackets — exists only to refine the behaviour of those three.

In an improvised build the boiling vessel is a stainless steel or enamel pot with a well-fitting lid; a domed or angled lid helps, because condensing droplets run to one edge instead of dripping straight back into the pot. A tube of copper or food-grade stainless steel leads vapour out to the condenser, which in the simplest form is a coil of that same tube — traditionally called the worm — sitting in a bucket of cold water. Vapour entering warm and leaving cool has nowhere to go but into the liquid phase, and drips from the low end into the receiver. Counter-flow cooling is better if it can be arranged: feeding the cooling water in at the far end so it travels against the vapour keeps the coldest water where the vapour is nearly liquid, and extracts far more heat per litre of coolant.

Desalinating water is the clearest demonstration of the principle. Bring salty or dirty water to a gentle boil at about 100 °C. Water molecules leave as vapour while salts, minerals, heavy metals, bacteria and viruses stay in the pot, because none of them has any meaningful vapour pressure at that temperature. What condenses is distillate: water free of dissolved solids and biologically sterile.

The most common error, and the one that quietly ruins a run, is boiling too hard. A violent boil throws a fine mist of unvaporised droplets up the vapour path alongside the true vapour — a fault called carryover or entrainment — and those droplets carry with them precisely the salts and contaminants the process exists to leave behind. A slow, steady boil with the thermometer holding rock-steady gives the purest product. If the liquid is visibly leaping in the pot, the heat is too high.

A solar still applies the same physics without fuel: a dark basin of water beneath a sloping transparent cover, sunlight evaporating the water and the cooler underside of the cover condensing it so it runs down to a collection channel at the low edge. The honest limitation is throughput. Even in strong sun a well-built solar still yields roughly 1 to 4 litres per square metre per day — enough to keep one person alive, nowhere near enough to supply a household.

sections.heading: Fractional Distillation and Separating Mixed Liquids
sections.body:
When two miscible liquids boil at temperatures close together, a single distillation gives a disappointing result: the vapour is enriched in the more volatile component, but only somewhat, and the distillate is still a mixture. Fractional distillation solves this by making the vapour repeat the separation many times over on its way out. A fractionating column — a vertical tube packed with glass beads, ceramic saddles or metal mesh, or fitted with a series of internal plates — is inserted between the boiling vessel and the condenser. Vapour rising through it cools slightly against the packing and partly re-condenses; that condensate trickles back down, meets rising hot vapour and is partly re-boiled. Each condense-and-re-boil cycle is a small distillation in its own right, and each leaves the vapour a little richer in the lower-boiling component. Column performance is counted in theoretical plates, one plate being one idealised equilibrium stage; a metre of well-packed column may be worth ten or more.

Reflux ratio is the other control. Some of the liquid condensing at the top can be returned down the column rather than collected, and the larger that returned fraction, the more thoroughly the column separates — at the price of collecting product more slowly. Taking product off fast with little reflux gives a quick, impure run; refluxing heavily gives a slow, sharp one. Petroleum refineries run enormous versions of exactly this, drawing gases off at the cool top of the tower, then naphtha, kerosene, diesel and heavy oils from progressively lower and hotter trays.

A worked example makes the limits visible. Ethanol boils at 78.4 °C and water at 100 °C, so vapour from a warm ethanol-water mixture is strongly ethanol-rich, and a good column drives it to roughly 95 per cent. It cannot go further, because at about 95.6 per cent ethanol by weight the pair forms an azeotrope — a constant-boiling mixture boiling at 78.2 °C whose vapour has precisely the same composition as the liquid. Once the two phases are identical in composition, additional plates accomplish nothing whatsoever, and no amount of redistillation raises the purity. Breaking through demands a different mechanism entirely: molecular sieves that adsorb water by pore size, a chemical drying agent, or a change in operating pressure that shifts where the azeotrope sits.

One caution belongs here plainly. Distilling alcohol for consumption is licensed or outright prohibited in many jurisdictions regardless of scale or intent, and this account of the chemistry is not an instruction to produce it. The general principle — that azeotropes impose hard purity ceilings on particular liquid pairs — matters far beyond alcohol, in solvent recovery, fuel blending and laboratory work alike.

sections.heading: Solvent Extraction: Pulling Compounds Out
sections.body:
Extraction is separation by preference rather than by boiling point. A target compound is coaxed into a solvent it dissolves in readily, while the material it came from, and the compounds nobody wants, stay behind.

Liquid-liquid extraction relies on two solvents that will not mix. Shake an aqueous mixture with an immiscible organic solvent and every dissolved compound distributes itself between the two layers according to its partition coefficient — the ratio of its concentration in one solvent to its concentration in the other once equilibrium is reached. A compound whose partition coefficient is 10 in favour of the organic layer ends up roughly 90 per cent extracted in a single shake with an equal volume, and a useful practical consequence follows from that arithmetic: three extractions using a third of the solvent each recover appreciably more than one extraction using the whole volume at once, because every pass re-establishes equilibrium against fresh, empty solvent. Let the layers settle completely, then draw off the one wanted; a separating funnel with a tap at the base makes the cut clean.

Solid-liquid extraction is the everyday kind, and the variables that matter are temperature, time, particle size and solvent choice. Infusion steeps a solid in hot solvent to pull out whatever dissolves quickly — roughly 1 to 2 grams of dried plant material per 200 millilitres of water at 90 to 100 °C for five to ten minutes is a standard herbal infusion. Decoction applies to tough, dense material such as roots and bark, where lignified cell walls resist and a low simmer of twenty to forty-five minutes is needed to get anything out at all.
